items.title: Incomplete product data can now hold up your EU orders
items.summary: Since 1st November 2026, items sold online from the UK to consumers in the EU need three product identifiers on their customs declaration, and the European Commission says the rule is enforced. At nShift, the multi-carrier shipping platform that connects retailers to more than 1,000 carriers, we hav
items.body:
Since 1st November 2026, items sold online from the UK to consumers in the EU need three product identifiers on their customs declaration, and the European Commission says the rule is enforced.
At nShift, the multi-carrier shipping platform that connects retailers to more than 1,000 carriers, we have already built support for them into our shipping software, so the remaining work is product data: getting each code out of the catalogue and onto every order. By Jacob Hopewell, Logistics and Retail Software Consultant at nShift.
A wool jumper sold to a shopper in Lyon has long carried a customs tariff (HS) code on its declaration. Now it also needs your own product code, the manufacturer’s code and, where the product has one, its barcode number. Book it through Royal Mail’s Click & Drop booking tool and a missing code stops the order at the booking screen: no postage is applied until your product SKU and the manufacturer’s ID are added, so the parcel waits with you.
Business-to-business shipments are “in principle not concerned”, according to the Commission’s guidance for member states and traders. For consumer orders, the identifiers apply whichever import VAT route a parcel takes, including the Import One-Stop Shop (IOSS), the EU’s VAT scheme for low-value parcels, which our IOSS explainer sets out in full. On value, the sources differ: the Commission’s guidance limits the rule to parcels worth up to 150 euro and says the law is being amended to match, but we have not found an adopted amendment yet. We advise sending the codes on every consumer shipment into the EU until the law is settled.
What a missing code costs
UPS warns that shipments without the codes “may be delayed, returned or incur a Pre-Release Notification Fee”, and DHL Express says customs “may be unable to release the shipment at the point of entry into the EU”. For your customer, that can mean a late parcel, or one that comes back to you with a fee attached. They add to the charges the EU’s customs reform has already brought in: a temporary 3 euro duty per item on consignments worth up to 150 euro and a 2 euro handling fee per item, both explained in our guide to the wider reform.
Where the codes get lost
I work with UK retailers on their delivery setup, and when a code goes missing, I expect to find the gap at one of three hand-offs: product record to order, order to shipping system, shipping system to carrier. The identifiers themselves usually exist.
The European Commission’s announcement points to product listings, invoices and packaging, which in most retail stacks means the catalogue, the product information management (PIM) system or the ERP.
A correct code can still be refused for its length. nShift’s transport management system (TMS) takes up to 70 characters per field, while the booking API of Posten Bring, the Norwegian postal company, rejects anything longer than 40. A 50-character code can pass one system and be refused by the next, so check the shortest limit among the carriers you book with.
Why the codes have to be right
The same announcement says the codes “will help customs authorities detect non-compliant and dangerous products more effectively and at scale”, so each one has to describe the real product. You assign your own product code, while the manufacturer’s code and the barcode number come from your supplier. Copying a SKU into the manufacturer’s field works only for products you make yourself. Where a product has no barcode, the declaration records that with Y081, the code for no standardised identifier, and either your declarant (the party that files the customs declaration) or your carrier enters it.
The cost of waiting
FedEx expects EU member states to allow a transition period until early 2027, yet it asks shippers to keep providing the codes without delay. Waiting means peak-season parcels ship with whatever gaps your data has today, and UPS and DHL Express have said what happens to those.
One stopgap is to type the codes into each booking screen as orders come in. It holds for a single carrier, and every new one means keying the same data again. The Commission also expects fuller product data requirements in July 2028, once the EU Customs Data Hub, its planned central system for e-commerce customs data, is deployed. Store the codes once in the product record and map them to your shipping system, and it sends them with each booking. They will also be in the record when the 2028 requirements arrive.
Where nShift helps
In nShift, you add the codes in the same place you manage shipments. Five nShift products have fields for them today, with coverage depending on the product and the carrier service, and our carrier-by-carrier guide to EU product identifiers shows where the codes go in each one.
Holding the codes in one place helps most when a retailer grows by adding carriers. Superdry ships from 21 websites to over 100 countries, and Gordon Knox, its Business Transformation and Logistics Director, says: “A growing international business such as Superdry needs to be able to put carriers onto our platform very quickly.” Its nShift system went live in the UK and Europe within four months.
About the author
Jacob Hopewell is a Logistics and Retail Software Consultant at nShift, the global leader in multi-carrier shipping and delivery experience. He works with UK retailers and brands on delivery across checkout, shipping, tracking and returns. The nShift platform connects to over 1,000 carriers and supports over one billion shipments a year.

items.title: Coles investigates cyber-attack and apologises to customers
items.summary: Supermarket giant says no customer, team or supplier data compromised but recommends updating passwords as a precaution Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised. Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts. Continue reading...
items.body:
Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised.
Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts.
“Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident,” the company said in a statement to the stock exchange.
“We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles’ systems.
“Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online.”
Coles apologised to its customers for any concerns they might have at “a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world”.
“We have security measures in place to protect customer and supplier accounts and are continuing to closely monitor our system,” it said.
“We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reuse the same password across multiple services.”
Coles also warned customers to be cautious if they received unexpected emails or SMS messages purporting to be from the retailer, and not to click any links.
In a separate and unrelated incident, Woolworths said it was aware of reports from customers who purchased compromised e-gift cards. The ABC first reported on Monday some customers had lost hundreds of dollars after buying the company’s Everyday WISH gift cards through its rewards website or app, only to find the sums loaded on to them had been spent by someone else.
Some customers told the national broadcaster they had lost up to $500, with transactions showing up at stores in different states to where they purchased the cards.
“We are aware of reports of an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and are looking into the matter as a priority,” a Woolworths spokesperson said in a statement. “We recognise the concern this has caused affected customers and we apologise to customers impacted. We encourage any customer who notices a transaction they don’t recognise to contact our Gift Card Support team.”
The company says it is working through all reported issues and will look into replacing affected e-gift cards.
– Additional reporting by Nick Visser

items.title: Poundland pins rescue hopes on Yorkshire Tea, Pot Noodle and Gloria Gaynor
items.summary: Chain restocks stores in operation named after singer of I Will Survive, as US owners release some of withheld funds Poundland’s under-fire US owners have released funds to help the stricken discount chain restock shelves temporarily, keeping hopes of a rescue deal alive in the run-up to crunch talks with the government. In an emergency resupply effort codenamed “Operation Gloria” by senior Poundland staff, about 16m grocery items were dispatched to 600 shops in the UK and Ireland over the weekend. Continue reading...
items.body:
Poundland’s under-fire US owners have released funds to help the stricken discount chain restock shelves temporarily, keeping hopes of a rescue deal alive in the run-up to crunch talks with the government.
In an emergency resupply effort codenamed “Operation Gloria” by senior Poundland staff, about 16m grocery items were dispatched to 600 shops in the UK and Ireland over the weekend.
The name comes from the Gloria Gaynor song I Will Survive, which soundtracked a defiant video posted by Poundland on social media showing pallets of Yorkshire Tea and Pot Noodles making their way from depots to the shelves.
The US investment firm Gordon Brothers earlier agreed to unlock £21m of £50m that it had been withholding, amid accusations it was endangering the business.
The money will provide breathing space while rescue talks continue, ensuring that suppliers continue sending goods to branches during the crucial pre-Christmas trading period.
Poundland filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the end of last month, throwing the fate of its 12,000 staff and about 2,000 suppliers into uncertainty.
Last week the chain won approval from the high court for an extension of legal protection from creditors, giving it until 26 November to find a buyer.
The company and Gordon Brothers are now heading for a frantic period of talks with potential buyers and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds.
Discussions could be soured by allegations – denied by Gordon Brothers – that the US investment group is more interested in protecting its own interests by breaking up the business despite signs of a dramatic improvement in its trading performance.
Gordon Brothers bought Poundland from the Polish retail group Pepco last year for a nominal £1 and claims to have rescued the company from collapse when nobody else would.
However, the US business has faced criticism from MPs, who have accused it of “predatory capitalism” and extracting millions of pounds as Poundland found itself on a knife-edge.
Liam Byrne, the chair of the business select committee, has likened Gordon Brothers to “the wolf of Wall Street, on the British high street”.
Documents provided to MPs showed the finance firm had taken close to £20m in interest payments and various fees, including those relating to store closures, since acquiring Poundland.
Gordon Brothers has denied freezing any funds that should have been available to Poundland, and pointed to loans that it has provided to prop up the company.
Reynolds plans to meet Poundland and Gordon Brothers before the deadline to stave off administration runs out, according to a report by Sky News.
He and Andy Burnham have expressed concerns about Gordon Brothers’ conduct, with the prime minister asking why the US company has yet to accept an offer for a business that employs 11,000 people.
Poundland has said it is in discussions with three potential buyers.
Bids from the investment groups Xyra Group Holdings and Innovest are understood to have relatively little chance of success.
Martin Property Group, a Northern Irish company, is Poundland’s preferred bidder but progress has stalled over the repayment terms of a loan from Gordon Brothers.
A number of high-street retailers, including Tesco, are eyeing up some of Poundland’s shops.
A Gordon Brothers spokesperson said: “Funds will be released to allow payroll to be made in full this month, while additional funds continue to be released to support Poundland’s ongoing trading.
“While our preference remains a sale of the whole company, we are taking due care to ensure that any successful offer can provide the funds required to acquire the business and see it through to sustainable cash generation.”
The Guardian approached Poundland for comment. The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade declined to comment.

items.title: Labour blasted over 'shambolic' business rates system as firms flock to get revaluations
items.summary: April's three-yearly revaluation led to a big rise in bills for some firms, adding to the pressure of minimum wage and national insurance rises.
items.body:
Labour blasted over 'shambolic' business rates system as firms flock to get revaluations
Labour has been accused of running a ‘shambolic business rates system’ after officials ‘rolled over’ and cut bills in a quarter of cases where firms simply registered for a check of their revaluation, while others faced delays in assessments that may be endangering their operations.
April’s three-yearly revaluation led to a big rise in bills for some firms, adding to the pressure of minimum wage and national insurance rises.
Hospitality has been among sectors hit hardest, leading to the closure of pubs and restaurants.
A rate cut was given to 6,000 of the 24,880 businesses that sought a check of their revaluation between April and September and whose cases were resolved.
Separately 5,240 cases have progressed to a formal challenge, only 290 of which have been resolved.
Of those, nearly two-thirds, or 62 per cent, had their rates reduced. Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said: ‘This shows the shambolic business rates system is already in chaos.’
In total, 37,000 businesses in England and Wales have registered for checks of this year’s revaluation, with 11,000 yet to be dealt with.
Dire: Labour has been accused of running a ‘shambolic business rates system’
Officials aim to ‘complete all reviews within the statutory deadline of 18 months’. But Griffith said: ‘Eighteen-month waits and the backlog show they haven’t got a grip when Labour has raised rates, hurting the high street and jobs alike.
For many, these delays will be the final straw.’ Mike Warburton, a retired tax director with accountant Grant Thornton, said the levels of reductions being agreed to are almost a tacit ‘admission of overcharging’, adding: ‘It shows it is worth challenging.
'We’ve got restaurants and pubs, which are often at the centre of communities, closing thanks to factors like National Insurance and minimum wage rises. You get to a stage where you just can’t make a profit.’
Tina McKenzie, national chair of the Federation of Small Businesses, said: ‘The fact that nearly two-thirds of completed challenges were successful in lowering bills suggests many firms had legitimate concerns. It’s a warning sign to ministers.’
The figures also show how businesses unhappy after challenging their 2023 rateable values and went to an appeal finally had them cut in 53 per cent of cases.
HMRC said most outstanding 2023 valuation challenges were submitted in the past 12 to 18 months as they had until March 31 this year.
It is responsible for valuing 2.14 million business premises and said it did ‘everything it can to ensure all valuations are accurate’.
The Government said: ‘HMRC uses robust evidence and established industry methods to ensure rateable values are accurate, with the vast majority of checks resulting in no change.’
It said the Budget cut rates by 20 per cent for pubs, clubs and music venues, axing them for premises with a rateable value below £18,000.

items.title: Have cars become too fat for Britain's roads and parking spaces? We investigate the rise of 'carspreading'
items.summary: It's happened to every driver. You've parked in a supermarket space with empty bays on either side, but by the time you've returned with your shopping your car's flanked by two SUVs...
items.body:
Have cars become too fat for Britain's roads and parking spaces? We investigate the rise of 'carspreading'
It's happened to every driver. You've parked in a supermarket bay with empty spaces on either side, but by the time you've returned with your shopping, your car is now flanked by two enormous SUVs. And there's simply not enough room to open your door.
Campaigners have dubbed the phenomenon 'carspreading'. And the term has been officially recognised by Collins English Dictionary as 'the tendency of manufacturers to build cars that are longer, wider, and heavier'.
A recent YouGov poll found that three in five Britons think its SUVs specifically that are taking up too much space on our roads.
And it's not likely to get better any time soon. Drivers' appetite for these larger jacked-up motors has transformed the UK's car parc into a giant 4x4 playground, with the number of SUV models available surging by 543 per cent between 2000 and 2025, according to market research by CarGurus.
Some of the biggest are over two metres wide, leaving less than 20cm either side in a typical parking bay in Britain.
But it's not just an obsession with SUVs that's creating this squeeze. Even superminis, some of the smallest motors on the road, are growing.
Models such as the Volkswagen Polo are almost 20cm wider today than they were in the 1970s, which coincidentally was the last decade in which rules were set for minimum parking-bay dimensions of 2.4 metres wide and 4.8 metres long.
It begs the question: are new cars now simply too fat for Britain? This is Money investigates...
How fat is the average new car?
The average new car on sale today occupies one square metre more space than a new motor sold in 2006, according to Vehicle Data Global (VDG).
The same data shows the average vehicle footprint has increased by 12.3 per cent since 2006, rising from 7.67 square metres to 8.61 square metres.
VDG found that the rate at which cars are growing in size has doubled over the last decade compared with the period between 2006 and 2016.
And while the popularity of SUVs, which accounted for more than half of all car models on sale last year, receives most of the blame for what VDG calls 'the car growth phenomenon', it is not just larger vehicles that are getting bigger.
Even superminis are becoming far less mini. Britain's best-selling small car, the Vauxhall Corsa, has grown from a footprint of 6.01 square metres in 1995 to 7.17 square metres in 2026.
Similarly, the Volkswagen Golf family hatchback has seen its footprint increase by 12.4 per cent over the same period, expanding from 6.81 square metres in 1995 to 7.66 square metres in 2026.
In 2024, green think tank Transport & Environment (T&E) analysed historical UK car-market data and found that the average new model becomes 1cm wider every two years.
Then and now: Cars like the evergreen Range Rover have dramatically increased in scale. Today's luxury SUV (right) is a quarter of metre wider than the Seventies original (left)
Why are new cars fatter? Three reasons...
1. Stricter crash-safety regulations
The biggest factor behind the growth in vehicle size is undoubtedly safety and the drive to improve occupant protection.
Modern cars require crumple zones, stronger structures, additional airbags and an ever-growing array of safety technology, all of which take up space.
Manufacturers must build these features into their vehicles to comply with increasingly stringent regulations, meaning passenger cars of all types, not just SUVs, have expanded to accommodate them.
2. The unstoppable rise of the SUV
For decades, 4x4s were seen as agricultural workhorses rather than status symbols.
That began to change in 1970 with the launch of the original Range Rover, which combined luxury with genuine off-road capability and showed that such vehicles could be desirable as well as practical.
Luxury brands including Lexus, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Audi and Porsche soon followed suit, though SUVs largely remained the preserve of wealthier buyers.
That changed dramatically around the turn of the century as America's love affair with SUVs began to influence motorists in Britain. Then, in 2006, the arrival of the Nissan Qashqai turned the SUV into a mainstream family car and a genuine alternative to the traditional hatchback.
Fast forward almost two decades and more than one in three new vehicles joining Britain's roads today are SUVs or jacked-up 'crossovers', offering drivers a higher seating position, improved visibility and a greater sense of security.
3. Car industry greed
As well as appealing to buyers' vanity, SUVs have become a major profit generator for manufacturers.
While they are often marketed as premium products, the reality is that many two-wheel-drive SUVs are no larger than the hatchbacks on which they are based and frequently use the same engines and underpinnings. Their perceived status, however, allows car makers to charge substantially more.
Take the Ford Puma, for example. Britain's best-selling new car for the past three years offers broadly similar practicality to the Fiesta, yet was priced around 10 to 15 per cent higher than its supermini sibling before the Fiesta was axed in 2023.
Carspreading is causing a national parking crisis, according to experts. We take a closer look
Fat cars are causing a 'parking crisis'
While new motors are getting 1cm wider every two years, Britain's streets aren't. And that's creating significant headaches for drivers.
In 2024, T&E found that more than half of all new cars sold the previous year were too wide for the average 1.8-metre roadside parking bay.
VDG also discovered that four fewer vehicles can now be parked on a typical 200-metre residential street than two decades ago, with capacity falling from 94 vehicles in 2006 to 90 in 2026.
The trend is forcing some residents to park further from their homes and contributing to what VDG describes as a growing 'parking crisis'.
T&E has also predicted that Britain's towns and cities could see a 10 per cent reduction in roadside parking spaces by 2040 as vehicles continue to grow in size and 'oversized SUVs' become increasingly popular.
London alone is forecast to lose around 100,000 parking spaces.
As a result, the think tank has warned that expanding vehicle dimensions pose an 'unprecedented threat to urban space' that could 'eliminate vast numbers of parking spaces' over the next decade.
'After 25 years of relentless growth, our streets are dominated by oversized SUVs that cities simply weren't designed for,' explained Anna Krajinska, T&E's UK director.
'The result is a lose-lose: councils are forced to reshape streets around larger vehicles, sacrificing parking capacity, public space, and safety in the process.
'This is a market failure. Without clear standards to limit car size and encourage right-sizing, carspreading will continue unchecked, and cities will keep paying the price.'
London alone could lose 100,000 on-street parking spaces within 15 years if new vehicle sizes continue to grow at the same trajectory, T&E cautions
It's not just public parking spaces that modern SUVs are struggling to fit into.
Cars have become so large that many motorists no longer use their garages for their intended purpose.
The average single household single garage measures 2.53 metres wide and 5.18 metres long, dimensions that are increasingly unsuitable for many of today's new cars.
As a result, 37 per cent of motorists with a garage at home told insurer Churchill that they never use it to store a vehicle.
For more than two-fifths of those surveyed, the reason was simple: their car is so large that there is barely enough room to open the doors once it's parked inside.
The growing squeeze isn't just causing inconvenience. It's costing drivers money, too.
A study by Skoda estimates that Britons spend around £1.5billion a year repairing vehicle damage caused in car parks.
Much of the cost comes from paint touch-ups and minor dent repairs resulting from one car door striking another, as larger vehicles leave motorists with ever less room to manoeuvre in tight parking spaces.
Vehicle Data Global found that 1 in 22 kerbside parking spaces are lost to longer cars
It is believed that restrictions on vehicle sizes could save an estimated 2,500 lives by 2040
Does Britain need bigger parking spaces?
Britain faces a simple problem: parking-bay guidelines haven't changed for more than 50 years, while cars have continued to grow.
The recommended size for a standard public parking bay remains 8ft (2.4m) wide and 16ft (4.8m) long, measurements introduced in the 1970s.
However, the British Parking Association says these dimensions are 'neither minimum nor written in tablets of stone', meaning councils and car park operators are free to set their own bay sizes.
But if local authorities, supermarkets and private car park companies decide to make spaces bigger, what would that mean for availability?
To accommodate today's larger vehicles, the average parking bay would need to increase from 4.8m to 5m in length and from 2.4m to 2.6m in width.
The trade-off could be significant. Car retailer Motorpoint estimates that 11 per cent of UK parking bays would need to be removed to create larger spaces.
While bigger bays would make parking easier for owners of modern vehicles, they would also come at the cost of an estimated 1.3 million parking spaces nationwide.
To put this into perspective, Bluewater shopping centre in Kent would see it's 13,000 available spaces decline by 1,430 to just 11,570. Meadowhall in Sheffield would have to remove 1,320 bays from its 12,000 parking-space facilities, while Westfield London would have to make do with 440 fewer bays in its current 4,000 allocation.
Many motorists, however, appear willing to accept that compromise.
Motorpoint's own resarch found that almost three-fifths (59 per cent) of the 2,000 drivers surveyed believe parking spaces are now too narrow for modern cars, while a quarter think car parks should be redesigned to make parking easier.

| Shopping Centre | Location | Number of parking spaces | Number of parking spaces that could be lost | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Bluewater | Kent | 13,000 | 1,430 | 
| Meadowhall | Sheffield | 12,000 | 1,320 |

| Merry Hill | Dudley | 9,209 | 1,012 | 
| Westfield London | London | 4,000 | 440 |

'Carspreading is putting lives at risk'
Campaign group Clean Cities argues that the backlash against ever-larger cars is about far more than parking inconveniences. Safety, it says, is the real concern.
The bigger cars become, the greater the danger to pedestrians and cyclists. Research by the Vias Institute found that people struck by larger vehicles while walking or cycling are significantly less likely to survive.
Its analysis suggests pedestrians and cyclists are far more likely to be killed if they are hit by an SUV rather than a traditional hatchback or saloon.
Research by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) and Imperial College London found that vulnerable road users are 44 per cent more likely to die when struck by a 4x4-style vehicle than by a conventional car.
More alarming still, the figure rises to 82 per cent for children, the researchers found.
The LSHTM analysed data from more than 680,000 road collisions over a 35-year period, during which SUVs surged in popularity.
A key factor behind the increased risk is the SUV's greater height. The taller front end means pedestrians and cyclists are struck higher on the body, increasing the likelihood of serious or fatal injuries.
The report also noted that SUVs typically feature more upright grilles and squared-off bumpers. This blunter design makes a person more likely to be thrown forwards after impact, increasing the risk of being hit a second time or dragged beneath the vehicle.
On behalf of T&E Loughborough University found that for a driver of a Land Rover Defender, the high bonnet blocks their view of children up to 4.5 years
T&E's analysis of the new car market found that the average bonnet height of a passenger car sold in the UK has jumped from 77cm in 2010 to 84cm in 2024
Caz Conneller, UK campaign manager at Clean Cities, says: 'Carspreading has serious implications for road safety and public space. If cars continue to grow at the current rate there could be 40 per cent more child pedestrian fatalities by 2040, as bigger, heavier cars do more damage in a crash.
'A pressing concern is that drivers can't see young children over increasingly high-bonneted cars. This trend for larger cars is dangerously out of control.
'Bigger cars aren’t just dangerous - they also cause more havoc on our roads by reducing parking spaces, worsening traffic and clogging up our narrow streets and country lanes.
'We need to discourage ever bigger cars with fairer parking policies and stronger regulations on car-size and child-visibility.
'It would be great to see the trend move to innovative medium-sized models that still meet family needs without posing risks to vulnerable road users.'
The environmental impact of larger motors
Larger cars are not only taking up more space on Britain's roads, they're leaving a bigger environmental footprint, experts warn.
A report from the International Energy Agency (IEA) believes SUVs were responsible for 'over 20 per cent of the growth in global energy-related CO2 emissions' in 2023.
The agency made the stark claim that: 'If SUVs were a country, they would be the world's fifth largest emitter of CO2.'
The report also warned that the shift towards larger, heavier and less fuel-efficient vehicles is increasing demand for energy and raw materials alike.
'The trend towards heavier and less fuel-efficient cars increases energy demand, including oil and electricity use, as well as demand for basic metals and critical minerals needed for battery production.,' it said.
'Over the course of 2022 and 2023, global oil consumption directly related to SUVs rose by a total of over 600,000 barrels per day, accounting for more than a quarter of the overall annual growth in oil demand,' the report added.
If SUVs were a country, they would be the world's fifth largest emitter of carbon dioxide behind China, USA, India and Russia, the IEA says
Parisians voted last year to muscle SUVs off the French capital's streets by making them three times more expensive to park, and called on London to follow suit
Should the widest cars be taxed more?
Ahead of John Healey's inaugural Autumn Budget last month, Tory MPs warned that the Chancellor was considering a new tax on larger vehicles following lobbying from T&E.
Under the proposal, buyers of new SUVs, heavier saloons and larger hatchbacks would have faced an additional first-year Vehicle Excise Duty charge, commonly known as a showroom tax.
T&E has called for a supplementary levy of £10 per kilogram above specified weight thresholds, set at 1,600kg for new petrol and diesel cars and 2,000kg for electric vehicles.
Shadow Secretary of State for Transport Richard Holden told the Daily Mail in October that Labour could even take a vehicle's width into account when calculating any additional tax charge.
In the end, however, the proposals failed to materialise.
That said, some local authorities are already charging more for larger vehicles.
Cardiff Council, for example, imposes a parking-permit surcharge on what it describes as 'oversized and highly polluting vehicles'. Drivers with cars weighing more than 2,400kg pay higher permit fees, while vehicles exceeding 3,500kg are not eligible for permits at all.
Elsewhere in Europe, Paris has taken an even tougher approach. Parking charges for SUVs have been trebled as part of a wider effort to discourage their use in the French capital.
London Mayor Sadiq Khan has welcomed the Paris policy and said he will monitor its effectiveness closely, fuelling speculation that a similar crackdown on larger vehicles could one day be considered in the capital.

items.title: Gymshark in trademark battle that threatens future of small fitness business
items.summary: Exclusive: British sportswear firm is seeking to obtain rights to The Conditioning Club, which is also the name of a Gloucestershire gym Gymshark, the £1bn British sportswear firm started in a family garage , is locked in a trademark battle that threatens the future of a small fitness business. Ben Francis, the university dropout who started sewing his own gym clothes in his parents’ garage and is now estimated to be worth £800m, is trying to add The Conditioning Club to his Gymshark stable of trademarks. Continue reading...
items.body:
Gymshark, the £1bn British sportswear firm started in a family garage, is locked in a trademark battle that threatens the future of a small fitness business.
Ben Francis, the university dropout who started sewing his own gym clothes in his parents’ garage and is now estimated to be worth £800m, is trying to add The Conditioning Club to his Gymshark stable of trademarks.
However, The Conditioning Club is also the name of a gym and fitness business based on an industrial estate in the Gloucestershire town of Fairford.
Founded by John Watson, who is the same age as 34-year-old Francis, the company registered its name at the UK Intellectual Property Office (UKIPO) for gym and fitness services five years ago.
Watson, who has nine staff and three self-employed personal trainers serving about 500 members, is now awaiting the outcome of proceedings by the UKIPO.
“When I registered our name, I thought I had done what I needed to do to protect us,” says Watson. “Five years later, we have members, employees, premises, relationships with schools and sports clubs and a genuine local community built around The Conditioning Club name.
“I never imagined that I would find myself having to defend our name, particularly against a business like Gymshark, which like us started from humble beginnings. I had previously looked to Ben and Gymshark as an example of what a small UK fitness-related business can achieve.”
Francis founded Gymshark in 2012 and US private equity firm General Atlantic took a stake in 2020, making the company a “unicorn” with a £1.25bn valuation and Francis a multimillionaire while still in his 20s. He was the recipient of an MBE for services to the commerce and the economy at 30.
In March 2025, Gymshark applied to register Conditioning Club and The Conditioning Club as trademarks to offer services in classes including clothing, retail and entertainment services.
While Gymshark did not apply for a trademark covering fitness and training services, one of its applications is in the same class as Watson’s, as he had been selling branded gear for a number of years.
Watson moved to oppose the trademark application in the class he has registered to protect his brand. He also applied to extend his trademark to cover the classes, such as retail, that Gymshark had applied for that he had not thought to register when he set up his business.
Gymshark opposed him and also applied to the UKIPO to invalidate his original trademark ownership on the grounds that The Conditioning Club name is descriptive, essentially too generic and not distinct enough to be allowed to be trademarked.
However, Gymshark has multiple trademark registrations for the equally generic “Lifting Club” brand.
Watson’s legal costs are climbing towards £30,000. He recently launched a crowdfunding campaign via CrowdJustice. It has raised just over £5,000 to help.
“It feels deeply intimidating, the financial imbalance between us is enormous,” he said. “They can afford a prolonged trademark battle. It is a very David and Goliath situation. I’m happy to agree a sensible arrangement with them. This is about something much simpler: protecting the name of the business I created and have spent the last five years building.”
A legal battle stretching to almost 18 months with a small player in the fitness industry is at odds with the ethos and brand image on which Gymshark has built its name.
Earlier this week, the company donated £10,000 to the owner of a gym in Redditch that burned down.
Other acts of generosity include donating almost £9,000 to help a British athlete raise funds to achieve his dream of getting to the Olympics, after the long jumper had been forced to get a job as a delivery driver to continue training.
Gymshark declined to comment on the trademark battle.

items.title: David Jones’ future looks grim. Is Myer next?
items.summary: With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast When the retailer’s doors slide open, shoppers are greeted by rows of slashed price tags, frantic discounting, and all the other hallmarks of a department store closing down. Except this isn’t David Jones, the embattled upmarket retailer that is shutting half its 38 stores . Continue reading...
items.body:
When the retailer’s doors slide open, shoppers are greeted by rows of slashed price tags, frantic discounting, and all the other hallmarks of a department store closing down.
Except this isn’t David Jones, the embattled upmarket retailer that is shutting half its 38 stores.
This is its longtime rival, Myer, where entire floors are seemingly permanently on sale.
With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question: is Myer next?
‘Sustained erosion of relevance’
At first glance, Myer’s headline numbers seem to defy the retail gloom, with double-digit sales growth to $4.1bn last financial year.
That lift, however, was not driven by surging demand, but by adding sales from the newly acquired apparel chains, Just Jeans, Jay Jays, Portmans, Dotti and Jacqui E, bought from billionaire businessman Solomon Lew’s Premier Investments.
Meanwhile, to keep registers ringing, Myer employed “higher than planned promotional activity to stimulate demand”, according to its annual report, which reduced its profitability.
The department store has also slashed the value of its brands, down more than $200m in one year alone, in an admission that its labels are worth far less than they once were.
Department stores have faced a “sustained erosion of relevance over the past five years”, according to IBISWorld market researchers, as online platforms win over bargain-hunters and specialists like beauty retailer Mecca prove more nimble in capturing shifting tastes.
DJs and Myer, on the other hand, have been weighed down by long-running physical property leases tied to underperforming stores in their sprawling networks.
The era of Australian families being fiercely loyal to either David Jones or Myer is long gone, replaced by a grim battle for both chains to stay relevant.
The stress on big department store profitability has been exacerbated by a period of cost of living pressures that have “entrenched deal-hunting behaviour, reshaping how and when consumers engage with department stores”, according to IBISWorld.
Myer was contacted for comment.
Survival tactic or slow-motion bankruptcy
Myer, however, has a critical advantage over David Jones: time.
While DJs fell into administration under mounting debts, Myer finished last financial year with a $100m net cash buffer, buying management breathing space to fix the business.
It has been reducing store numbers and with it lease liabilities – down to 56 stores from 60 before the pandemic – which is something David Jones is only doing now that it has collapsed into administration.
For the moment, Myer is leaning into the discounts demanded by shoppers, in the hope that more profitable trading conditions will emerge.
Richard Hemming, the editor at Under The Radar Report, says in retail “volume is everything”.
“If you get the volumes through, that customer base will eventually be in a position to pay more, and when volumes and margins both improve, you get that double effect,” Hemming says.
While analysts have mixed views on whether permanent discounting is a smart survival tactic or a slow-motion way to go bankrupt, department stores do need to move huge volumes of stock to keep cash flowing and clear seasonal goods.
They can use those discounts to get more people signed up to their loyalty programs – such as the successful Myer One scheme – in the hope they will become long-term customers.
Hemming sees the upside in Myer’s current pain, noting the retailer is “cleaning house earlier than rivals” precisely because investors have long priced it “like it’s going to go broke”.
Myer is revamping the business to aggressively pursue online sales.
Advantage over old rival
Myer shares have been heavily sold down over the years, and now hover around the 24c mark, representing a fraction of its $4.10 float price from 2009.
It did, however, receive a price bump on the day DJs fell into administration.
With roughly two in five Myer stores sharing a shopping centre with a David Jones outlet, investors are betting the coming closure of 19 DJs sites will hand Myer an easy market-share boost, even as its own long-term turnaround demands further store cuts.
In the short term, the pain is likely to intensify for Myer as the David Jones stores marked for closure are under orders to clear stock with widespread promotions, luring customers.
Broader retail sentiment is also souring, as a string of interest rate rises and escalating cost-of-living pressures force cash-strapped shoppers to pare their discretionary spend.
The Retail Doctor Group’s chief executive, Brian Walker, says the main long-term advantage Myer has over its old rival is financial flexibility.
“Whereas David Jones was incredibly encumbered, Myer doesn’t have that issue right now,” Walker says.
“As we sit here today, Myer is financially stronger, but strategically still pretty vulnerable.”

Episode details
Available for 27 days
Black Friday promises huge savings, but are the deals really as good as they seem? Before you click 'buy' Linzi Lima discusses the misleading discounts and marketing tactics that could leave shoppers paying more than they bargained for. Luxury serums, miracle ingredients and skincare routines costing hundreds of pounds. But when it comes to healthy skin, does a bigger price tag really mean better results? We separate the science from the hype... Why do some products just not last like they used to? Like trainers that fall apart after a few wears - many consumers feel quality is slipping. As trusted heritage brands change hands and manufacturing is outsourced, we investigate what's driving the decline and hear from the founder of the website 'Worse on Purpose' about the growing problem. Would you rather stream your music or own it? In an age of playlists and subscriptions, more people are returning to vinyl records, CDs and other physical formats. We'll explore what's behind the revival and why music fans are once again choosing something they can hold in their hands. Complaints about parcel deliveries are on the rise, and now Ofcom is warning companies to raise their game or face tighter regulation. We hear from James Stinson of Ofcom in Belfast. items.title: Could Comet return to the high street? New owner has ambitions to revive former electrical retail giant
items.summary: Electricals retailer Comet collapsed in 2012 and was one of the biggest high street casualties Britain has seen. Its new boss has big ambitions for the revived company.
items.body:
Could Comet return to the high street? New owner has ambitions to revive former electrical retail giant
Electricals retailer Comet collapsed in 2012 and was one of the biggest high street casualties Britain has ever seen.
It's now back, but online only, and its boss, Cas Paton, has major ambitions for the group.
Notably, he is not ruling out a return to the high street in Britain for Comet.
The 236-shop business, which at the time employed around 7,000 people, was acquired in 2011 for the nominal sum of £1 by private equity group OpCapita.
OpCapita failed to revive Comet's fortunes, as the retailer suffered amid the decline in consumer spending during the recession and the seismic growth of online rivals.
The chain collapsed in November 2012. Thousands of people lost their jobs and were left out of pocket as a result of the administration, and taxpayers had to foot a bill of approximately £50million for unpaid taxes and redundancy costs.
Comet, which was founded in Hull in 1933 and began life selling batteries and radios, was acquired by London-based online marketplace OnBuy in 2025.
Nothing ruled out: Cas Paton told This is Money he had not ruled out a return to the high street for Currys
OnBuy has said it wants to be a 'serious challenger' to rivals like Amazon and Currys.
Last year, OnBuy said it planned to resurrect Comet 'as a marketplace at the apex of e-commerce'.
This is Money asked Paton, founder and chief executive of OnBuy, if shoppers could expect to see Comet return to high streets across Britain.
Paton told This is Money: 'Never say never. We've launched online because that's the right model for Comet now, but I'd love to see the name back on British high streets in some form.
'We're already exploring partnerships that could make that happen.
'I don't think the answer is simply to recreate the old stores and pretend retail hasn't changed.
'It would have to be relevant, exciting and give people a reason to walk through the door.'
Paton said Comet had been revived as a 'specialist electricals marketplace, to be a modern-day champion of tech, gadgets, and built around how people actually want to shop now'.
He added: 'We are onboarding more suppliers and brands every day, so we expect the range, and the number of deals available, to keep growing over the coming months.'
The chief executive said shoppers 'did not need another website selling everything'.
He said: 'Britain needs great retail destinations that actually know what they stand for.
'If I'm looking for a new TV, laptop or washing machine, I want proper choice, a great price and a shopping experience built around electricals.
'More competition matters because it gives customers greater choice. It forces everyone to work harder on price, range and the experience they offer. That's healthy.'
Star deals: Comet collapsed in Britain in 2012, triggering thousands of job losses
Get what you can: A photo from 2012 of a Comet shop closing down
It's personal: For Cas Paton, the revival of Comet is personal as he visited the shops as a boy
Paton said he also believed the Government was not doing enough to support retailers.
He said: 'The Government is treating retailers as a source of revenue rather than an engine for growth.
'At the moment, businesses feel they are succeeding despite the system, not because of it.
'You can't keep increasing costs, adding regulation and then act surprised when shops close or investment goes elsewhere.
'Retailers need stability. They need to know that employing another person, opening another location or investing in better technology won't be punished by the next Budget.
'Stop trying to choose between online retail and the high street as well. The future is both.
'Give businesses the conditions to grow and let retailers work out how customers want to shop.'
For Paton, the revival of Comet is personal. He remembers visiting Comet's Trafford Park store with his late dad Nigel as a boy and being blown away by the technology on display.
So, Comet's back online, but it is operating in a tough environment. Competition from the likes of Amazon, Currys and AO World will not be going away any time soon.
There were 738,144 British businesses in 'significant' financial distress in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest quarterly 'red flag alert' report from BTG Consulting PLC, a Manchester-based insolvency adviser formerly known as Begbies Traynor.
It comes against a backdrop of rising inflation in Britain, with energy bills set to increase further in January 2027 as the impact of the Middle East energy shock continues to feed through into the cost of living.

items.title: Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank
items.summary: Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to bring shoppers back The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap? Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing. Continue reading...
items.body:
The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap?
Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing.
Central to this, the study says, is trying to banish, or at least tame, motor traffic, because too often urban centres are places “designed to be driven through, not for time to be spent in”.
As well as citing a lack of imagination, the report, which is co-produced by bike storage company Cyclehoop, blames planning regulations that favour conformity and clutter and too often treat speeding cars as a given, to which everything else must adjust.
“The default high street is engineered for traffic and furnished from a catalogue: a tarmac pavement, guardrails penning people at the kerb, litter bins ordered from a procurement catalogue, a row of plastic planters – public investment that is joyless,” it says.
While planners have traditionally focused on car access as a metric for thriving town centres, calculations for the Create Streets report suggest that replacing parking with other kerbside infrastructure, including bike spaces or outside drinking and dining areas, creates more economic value.
It found that one parking space in the high street of a market town is typically used by about 3.5 vehicles a day, bringing in just over £73,000 a year in spending to nearby shops.
But the same 12 square metres, if used to hold nine share e-bikes, generates an average of 13 trips a day, with over £146,000 a year in spending, even taking into account the lower average spend per person.
In a busier city, where share bikes would be used more frequently, the estimated total annual spend rises to more than £300,000.
Repurposing the space for outside dining brings less dramatic gains, but in a city centre it can still amount to about £120,000 in extra annual spending.
The report calls for a cultural rethink involving low-cost tweaks that rip away ugly and unnecessary street furniture and make better use of kerbsides.
Calling use by families “the indicator species of a healthy high street”, the report cites what is known as “the wrist test” – whether it feels safe to let go of a young child’s wrist so they can roam with some freedom.
This is best done, it argues, by removing the threat of speeding motor vehicles and not by trying to mitigate their impact. It calls the removal of pedestrian guardrails next to roads “the most cost-effective upgrade for the majority of high streets”, saying they are an eyesore with minimal safety benefits.
The report says “the absurdity of modern public realm management” is exemplified by Secured by Design, policy guidelines on cutting neighbourhood crime. These can, critics point out, mean benches and plants are removed on the advice of police, supposedly to discourage antisocial behaviour.
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, has pledged to try to reverse the decline of high streets, announcing in September a £210m regeneration fund.
However, the bulk of the money will go into buildings: turning old shops into shared workspaces or community cafes, or keeping pubs and clubs in business.
The report argues that renovating buildings is pointless if the street outside is unappealing. To reduce clutter, it says, there should be “a presumption of removal where an item cannot be justified”.
The effects can be dramatic, the report says, pointing to examples including Altrincham in Cheshire, where the creation of a walkable, car-free urban area helped see retail vacancies fall from over 30% to 7% in less than a decade.
Such initiatives do not have to be expensive, it claims, noting the example of an unused patch of land next to a church in Grimsby which was turned into a park for less than £20,000.
“Streets that are ugly are not so because councils lack the desire to change them, but because the system is counting the maintenance liabilities, not the benefits,” said David Milner of Create Streets.
“What works is cheap: trees in the ground, benches people want to sit on, clutter taken away.
“So much of what is built now seems to be temporary, looking more like road works than public realm improvements, so we encourage the concept of permanence; more trees in the ground, not in giant plant pots, for example.”
A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: “We support local leaders to make decisions on pedestrianisation based on their communities’ needs.
“Our Hope on the High Street strategy will help local people revive town centres by protecting community assets, bringing derelict buildings back into use and tackling the spread of vape and gambling shops.
“Funding is available for local leaders to spend on their priorities, including pedestrianising and regenerating their high streets if they so wish.”
